aspectTitle: Information conveyed exclusively by a CSS background-image (no img element, no DOM text equivalent)
aspectDescription: An element carries meaning purely through a CSS background-image — set in a stylesheet rule, an inline style= attribute, or injected by script — and that same meaning exists nowhere as real text in the DOM. Because there is no img/svg/object/input element and no alt slot, every ACT 1.1.1 rule (which is scoped to elements that can hold an accessible name) returns Inapplicable; there is no target to evaluate. A human must look at the rendered page, recognize that a background image is carrying information (a price banner, a status/stock icon, a 'SOLD OUT' stamp, a required-field marker, a weathe
scenario: Building-society loan card whose headline rate '19.3% APR Typical Variable' lives only as pixels in a stylesheet background-image SVG; the visible DOM prose says only 'Where else would you find a better interest rate?' (verbatim F3 example 1).
mechanism: The load-bearing price (19.3% APR Typical Variable) is rendered exclusively by `p#bestinterest { background-image: url(svg) }`. A CSS background image generates no accessibility-tree node and cannot carry a text alternative, so a screen-reader user hears the unanswered question and never learns the rate; forced-colors/hide-backgrounds drops it for sighted users too.

aspectTitle: A genuinely informative/functional image marked decorative (alt="" / role=presentation) so AT cannot reach it
aspectDescription: An image that actually conveys needed information or function is declared decorative — alt="", role=presentation, or role=none — so it is correctly hidden from AT per the markup and the ACT name-presence/decorative rules all PASS (the markup is internally consistent). The real failure is that the image SHOULD have carried a text alternative: it is the sole carrier of a fact or function (a 'Verified seller' badge, a size chart, a signature image, the only diagram of a recipe step, a wizard progress meter, a severe-weather pictogram). Detecting this requires viewing the rendered image, judging t
scenario: Marketplace listing whose 'Verified seller' green-check badge — the only per-listing signal that this seller passed identity verification — is an inline SVG suppressed from AT via role=presentation + aria-hidden. Unverified sellers render the same row without the check, so the badge's presence is the data; no text states this seller is verified.
mechanism: Informative trust badge declared decorative: the wrapper span carries role=presentation and the SVG aria-hidden=true, so the verification fact is pruned from the accessibility tree though it is the sole per-listing carrier (Trusted Tester 7.B condition 1 fails; F38/F39 inverted).

aspectTitle: Non-empty alt that is not actually an alternative: filename, placeholder, or auto-generated label (F30)
aspectDescription: An image has a non-empty accessible name that LOOKS like content but is not a usable substitute for the image: a filename ('DSC_0481.jpg', 'hero-2.png', 'banner_final_v3'), a CMS auto-caption ('image', 'photo', 'picture'), a programming reference ('img_001', 'Intro#2'), or an upload artifact ('Screenshot 2024-03-11 at 14.22.png'). Because the string is non-empty, every ACT presence rule PASSES. The descriptive-name rule (qt1vmo) only catches this if the placeholder happens to name a DIFFERENT identifiable asset; a filename like 'IMG_4823.jpg' on a sunset photo names nothing identifiable, so qt
scenario: Local-news article hero photo depicting a transit-fare protest (crowd marching past a domed City Hall, banners reading 'FAIR FARES'/'NO HIKE') whose alt is the raw DSLR camera filename alt="DSC_0481.JPG".
mechanism: Image accessible name is computed from alt = 'DSC_0481.JPG'; a screen reader announces a camera filename instead of the protest scene, so the alternative cannot substitute for the photo (F30 filename non-alternative).

aspectTitle: Alt literally describes the image but is wrong for the image's purpose-in-context (link target or control function)
aspectDescription: An image has an alt that correctly identifies the depicted thing — so it passes presence rules and even passes qt1vmo (it IS descriptive of the image in isolation) — but it is the WRONG alternative for the role the image plays on this page. The Understanding doc makes this explicit: the SAME globe image needs alt 'International Travel' on a travel site but 'International Campuses' on a university site; a newspaper-front-page thumbnail that links to a homepage needs the publication name, not a description of the masthead photo. The same applies to images used AS controls: a printer icon button
scenario: News aggregator grid: a newspaper front-page thumbnail is the sole content of a link to the publication's homepage, but its alt accurately describes the cover PHOTO ('Front page photo of a flooded town square under grey skies') instead of naming the publication. A correctly-labelled card (alt='The Harbor Gazette') is included for contrast.
mechanism: Because the is the only content of the , the image alt becomes the link's accessible name. The link to The Riverside Courier is therefore named for the cover photograph, not the publication, so the alternative does not serve the link's purpose-in-context (G94/H30 linked-thumbnail rule).

aspectTitle: Complex image (chart/diagram/map) has a plausible alt/long description that drops information the image conveys (F67)

aspectTitle: Image of meaningful text whose alt does not reproduce the same text
aspectDescription: An image whose primary content IS text — a logo wordmark, a quote rendered as a graphic, a pull-quote image, a 'terms' graphic, a scanned notice, a price/coupon banner that is essentially words — has a non-empty alt that describes or summarizes the image instead of reproducing the words. Because the alt is non-empty it passes presence rules, and because it may correctly identify the image ('promotional banner') it can pass qt1vmo, yet a screen-reader user never receives the actual text the image displays. For an image of meaningful text the alternative must contain the SAME text. Distinguishin
scenario: Marketing-email promo banner rendered as a flattened image (inline-SVG data: URI). aspectTitle: Text look-alike (homoglyph / Unicode confusable) glyphs representing text with no text alternative (F71)
aspectDescription: Visible 'text' on the page is actually composed of characters from another script chosen because their glyphs LOOK like the intended letters/digits — Cyrillic 'о' for Latin 'o', Greek 'ϲ' for 'c', Cyrillic letter for '3'. Sighted users read the intended word; a screen reader reads garbled output or silence because the codepoints are not the letters they resemble. Per F71 this is effectively non-text content (the meaning rides on glyph shapes, not the actual characters) and it lacks the required text alternative. No img/svg/object element is involved, so all ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable. Ca

scenario: Long-tail variant: a portfolio hero displays the designer's name 'Sumi Tanaka' (Mathematical Sans-Serif Bold, U+1D5E6 etc.) and role 'Designer & Illustrator' (Mathematical Sans-Serif Italic) pasted from a social-bio 'fancy text' generator; these are Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols whose glyphs only resemble Latin letters, with no plain-Latin text alternative.
mechanism: Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols are math-notation code points, not alphabet letters; most TTS engines either announce each glyph by its verbose Unicode name ('mathematical sans-serif bold capital S, ...') or skip them as unknown, so a screen reader never hears 'Sumi Tanaka, Designer and Illustrator' — the whole point of the profile — and no text alternative exists. Same SC limb as classic F71: meaning rides on glyph shape, not the encoded characters.

aspectTitle: Text look-alike (homoglyph / Unicode confusable) glyphs representing text with no text alternative (F71)
aspectDescription: Visible 'text' on the page is actually composed of characters from another script chosen because their glyphs LOOK like the intended letters/digits — Cyrillic 'о' for Latin 'o', Greek 'ϲ' for 'c', Cyrillic letter for '3'. Sighted users read the intended word; a screen reader reads garbled output or silence because the codepoints are not the letters they resemble. Per F71 this is effectively non-text content (the meaning rides on glyph shapes, not the actual characters) and it lacks the required text alternative. No img/svg/object element is involved, so all ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable. Ca
scenario: Boundary/PASS control on a kitchen-knife page: (A) the hero heading visually reads 'Cook' using confusable glyphs (U+03F2 U+043E U+03BF + k) but marks them aria-hidden and supplies a visually-hidden real-Latin 'Cook' text alternative; (B) a recipe quotes legitimate, language-tagged Greek (τζατζίκι and Καλή όρεξη, lang=el); (C) plain-Latin brand and CTA controls.
mechanism: The aria-hidden confusable glyphs are skipped by AT and the sr-only span exposes the real word, so the heading is announced as 'Cook well, eat well.'; the Greek spans are tagged lang=el and announced correctly as Greek. No range of text relies on look-alike glyphs without an alternative, so F71's failure condition ('there is not a text alternative for any range of text that uses look-alike glyphs') is not triggered.
